evidence:
The will is a typed one-page document dated 9 days before Lakshmi's death, signed with a shaky signature and witnessed by two people: the hospital's administrative clerk and Suresh's friend. It was not registered. Hospital records show Lakshmi was admitted for kidney failure and was receiving sedatives and pain medication, and a nursing note from the day before the will records her as "intermittently confused, oriented to person only." There is no doctor's certificate of capacity on the day of signing.

An earlier handwritten note from 6 years ago, found by Anita in a family album, says "all three children should share equally," but it is unwitnessed and unsigned beyond initials. Suresh's bank statements show he paid most of the hospital bills, which supports his caregiving claim. A cousin states that Suresh asked Lakshmi to "sign something" in hospital and she "didn't seem to know what it was," but the cousin was not present for the signing. The property listing for the land is already live online, and the municipal record shows Suresh's mutation application filed three weeks ago, still pending.

events.description: Lakshmi Reddy, 68, owned a house and a small plot of agricultural land.
She died 14 months ago, leaving three adult children: Suresh, who lived with her and cared for her in her final years, Anita, who lives abroad, and Kiran, who lives in another city.
Two weeks before her death, while she was in hospital, a will was reportedly signed in Suresh's favor, leaving him the house and the land, with a small cash sum for each sibling.
Anita and Kiran learned about the will only after the funeral and are shocked because Lakshmi had told both of them for years that the property would be divided equally.
Anita and Kiran suspect the will was signed when Lakshmi was too ill and medicated to understand it, and that Suresh influenced her.
Suresh responds that he did everything for his mother while the others "visited twice a year," that she freely chose to reward him, and that the will was properly witnessed.
He has already begun the process of mutating the property in his name and has put the land on the market.
Anita and Kiran want to know whether they can contest the will, whether they can stop the sale immediately, and what their realistic chances are.

evidence_plan.heading: Evidence plan
prompts: Which part of the timeline needs independent support?
What already shows that event, and who may lawfully hold another record?

suggestions.title: Possession, title and notices
suggestions.look_for: Gather records you already hold, such as agreements, deeds, orders, rent payments or notices. Note who occupied the property and when that changed.
suggestions.why: Documents and the timeline can help distinguish possession from a claim about legal ownership.
suggestions.action: Keep full copies and record where each came from. Request records through the issuing office or a lawyer when needed.

suggestions.title: Location and visible changes
suggestions.look_for: Note the address or boundary reference and any changed lock, barrier or damage you actually observed.
suggestions.why: This helps identify the location and the particular change in dispute.
suggestions.action: Document only from an area you may safely and lawfully access. Do not enter disputed space or confront anyone.

suggestions.title: Original records and an evidence log
suggestions.look_for: Keep records you lawfully have, with their surrounding context. For each item note the related event, who provided it, when you received it, and any transfer.
suggestions.why: The log distinguishes what you observed from what someone later told you and makes it easier to check the source.
suggestions.action: Keep an unchanged original and label working copies. Avoid editing originals, guessing gaps, or sharing evidence publicly.

suggestions.title: Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy
suggestions.reference: Civil Appeal 6191 of 2001 · para. 17, PDF pp. 6–7
suggestions.takeaway: The Court distinguished interference with possession from disputes where title or recovery of possession also needs to be decided.
suggestions.difference: Compare who possessed the property, whether title is seriously disputed, and the relief sought. The decision concerned competing claims to vacant plots.
suggestions.connection: Your account raises an issue about possession, ownership or interference with land.
suggestions.preparation: Work out who currently has possession, whether ownership is disputed and what order you want the court to make.
